title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam in which fraudsters pose as a named public figure and her colleagues to solicit payments from people who believe they are being offered a legitimate media appearance. The failure is not in a deployed AI product but in the use of AI as a tool by human actors: cybersecurity experts cited in the reporting say AI has made the fraudulent messages more personalized and plausible than earlier generations of such scams. The deception operates at the point of first contact, in an unsolicited email, before any institutional system has a chance to intervene.

What would have caught it earlier is a basic procedural check: the targeted individuals had no independent way to verify the invitation without contacting the real organization directly, and the fraudulent emails used unofficial addresses that did not match the broadcaster's domain. The personalization, which referenced recipients' specific work, reduced the instinctive suspicion that cruder mass-phishing generates.

It is not established who is responsible, what AI tools if any were used to draft or personalize the messages, or how many people paid money before recognizing the fraud. The investigations by WHYY, NPR, and law enforcement are ongoing, and no findings or charges have been reported.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other staff members of WHYY's "Fresh Air" program to defraud people seeking interview opportunities. The fraudulent emails, which are highly personalized and reference the recipient's work, ask targets to pay fees for production costs or offer compensation for interviews. Authors, entertainers and public figures have reported receiving these messages, with some emails coming from accounts like "terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com." One university professor initially believed she had been invited to discuss her recent book before suspecting fraud when asked to pay $250.

WHYY, NPR and law enforcement are investigating the scam and have stated they never charge guests for interviews. Cybersecurity experts note that artificial intelligence has made such impersonations more convincing and personalized than traditional scams. Red flags include requests for payment, a major show's host handling logistics personally, and emails from unofficial addresses. Victims are advised to verify interview requests directly with the organization rather than responding to suspicious messages.
